name: Tribulus terrestris

lead: Tribulus is a spiny plant whose extracts are sold as testosterone and libido supplements.
Controlled human studies have not consistently shown a testosterone effect, and no high-quality trial supports strength gains.

paras: Marketing points to steroidal saponins such as protodioscin; supporting evidence is mainly from rodent and primate studies.
Safety in humans has not been proven according to the NCCIH. Sheep suffer photodermatitis from the plant; confirmed human reactions are not documented.

lead: Tribulus terrestris (puncture vine, goathead) is a spiny annual plant of the caltrop family, native to warm regions of Eurasia and Africa and invasive elsewhere [1][2]. Its fruit and leaf extracts have been used in traditional Chinese and Ayurvedic medicine and have been sold since the 1980s as a supplement intended to raise testosterone for bodybuilding or sexual function [1][3].

Published controlled studies have not consistently shown a testosterone effect in humans, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health states it has not been proven safe, according to Wikipedia [1]. The Australian Institute of Sport discourages athlete use [1].
infobox: Dietary supplement; noxious weed in places [1]

paras: Linnaeus described the species in 1753 [1][2]. Grokipedia lists traditional uses as a diuretic, tonic, aphrodisiac and remedy for urinary complaints, with the plant used across Asia, Europe and Africa [2]. The Ayurvedic name Gokshura refers to a cow's hoof [2].

Extracts, usually standardised for steroidal saponins such as protodioscin, are marketed as testosterone boosters and libido aids [1][3]. Rat research reported that a protodioscin-containing extract affected sexual behaviour and intracavernous pressure in normal and castrated rats [4], and a primate/rabbit/rat study examined hormonal effects relevant to erectile dysfunction [5]. These are animal studies.

Wikipedia notes that the plant causes photodermatitis (geeldikkop) in sheep and that adverse reactions in humans have not been confirmed; a claim of liver damage at high doses carries a citation-needed tag [1]. Products are not pre-approved in the US, and the NCCIH says safety has not been proven [1].

A 2024 Annals of Internal Medicine evidence map found two low-quality trials of the plant for menopausal sexual symptoms, too varied to support conclusions [1]. Registered trials include studies in women with low sexual desire [6][7][8], a trial in men with oligospermia [9] and a 2025 study of acute anaerobic power in combat-sport athletes [10]. No high-quality randomised trial of strength or anabolic effects was identified by Wikipedia's review [1].

timeline.event: Extracts begin to be sold as testosterone-boosting supplements [1].
Evidence map finds only two low-quality trials in menopausal sexual symptoms [1].
